newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street experts split on Fed's next rate move.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street experts split on Fed's next rate move.

text.p: Wall Street experts lauded the Federal Reserve's handling of monetary policy on Wednesday but differed over what the central bank should do next.

In testimony to the House Banking Committee, two of three economists -- William Brown of J.P. Morgan and Co and Robert DiClemente of Salomon Brothers Inc -- suggested that the central bank needed to raise rates further.
But John Lipsky, chief economist for Chase Manhattan Bank, disagreed and said it was "conceivable" that the Fed's next interest rate move would be down rather than up.

In a bid to keep inflation in check and thus lengthen the economic expansion, the Fed raised short-term rates in March for the first time in more than two years, bumping them up a quarter percentage point.
It has since held rates steady against a backdrop of what Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan described this week as an "exceptional" economy of solid growth and low inflation.

"The Federal Reserve faces some signficant challenges in the months ahead," Salomon's DiClemente said. "Rapid growth in nominal demand over the past year may be symptomatic of an overly accomodative monetary policy that will need to be repositioned."
He suggested that the federal funds rate may need to be raised to over six percent, from 5-1/2 percent now.

"The current euphoria in the financial markets increasingly reflects a mistaken, and potentially harmful, view that any limits on the economy's capacity to grow without strain have been repealed," he said.
"It would be highly imprudent for the Fed to assume that the limits to growth have been removed."

J.P. Morgan's Brown agreed on the need for higher rates and urged the central bank to "balance the surging optimism in the private sector" in order to hold expansion to a sustainable pace. "What is needed now is not another cheerleader, but a dose of restraint," he said.
However, Chase Manhattan's Lipsky argued that the economy had undergone "favorable structural shifts."

Four factors have contributed to the low-inflation expansion of late, he said: sustained anti-inflationary monetary policy, economic liberalization, shrinking budget deficits and improved inventory controls.
"The prospects are good ... for continued moderate growth and quiescent inflation pressures," Lipsky said. "The Fed may not need to tighten policy further in this expansion phase."
"Indeed, it is conceivable that in time the Fed's next policy decision could be an easing," he added.

Besides hearing from the Wall Street experts, the House panel also took testimony from representatives from business, labor and academia, as well as from the Fed. The hearing was timed to coincide with Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress.
